question: I already validate my form inputs with a strict regex before building the SQL query by hand -- does passing that validation mean it's fine to just concatenate the values into the SQL string?
answer: No. Validating a value's type, length, or format does not make it safe to concatenate into SQL. You must still bind every data value through parameterized queries/prepared statements, regardless of how strictly it was validated beforehand.
source_section: Primary Defenses > Allow-List Input Validation
source_passage: Continue binding all data values, even when they pass type, length, or format checks. Validation of a value does not make it safe to concatenate into SQL.

question: We have a login page and a sign-up page hitting the same users table -- what's the recommended way to split up database account privileges so that a compromise of one page can't be used to write data through the other?
answer: Give each application (or each distinct function) its own dedicated database user account rather than sharing one owner/admin account. Grant only the access that function needs: for example, a login page should get read-only access to the username/password fields (no insert, update, or delete), while the sign-up page gets insert privilege on that table -- a separation that can only be enforced if the two pages connect as different DB users.
source_section: Hardening > Least Privilege > Least Admin Privileges For Multiple DBs
source_passage: As an example, a login page requires read access to the username and password fields of a table, but no write access of any form (no insert, update, or delete). However, the sign-up page certainly requires insert privilege to that table; this restriction can only be enforced if these web apps use different DB users to connect to the database.

question: I set my session cookie to SameSite=Lax -- am I covered against CSRF even if one of my endpoints still mutates data on a GET request?
answer: No. SameSite=Lax still allows the cookie to be sent on cross-site top-level navigations using safe methods (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE), so if any state-changing action in your app is reachable via GET, SameSite=Lax will not stop CSRF against it -- this is called out as the single most common way SameSite-based defenses fail in practice.
source_section: Defense In Depth Techniques > SameSite (Cookie Attribute) > Limitations of SameSite
source_passage: **`Lax` only blocks unsafe methods.** The default `Lax` behavior still allows the cookie on top-level navigations that use [safe methods](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7231#section-4.2.1) (`GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`, `TRACE`). If any state-changing operation in the application is reachable via a `GET` request, `SameSite=Lax` will not stop it. This is the single most common way `SameSite`-based defenses fail in practice. Review every `GET` endpoint and ensure that none of them mutate server-side state.

question: what's the actual difference between CSRF and SSRF -- and do they need different fixes, or can one set of defenses cover both?
answer: CSRF tricks an authenticated user's browser into an unwanted action on a trusted site; browser requests automatically include cookies, including session cookies. SSRF abuses the application itself to interact with internal or external networks or the machine, for example by fetching a user-supplied image URL or webhook destination. They affect different request paths, so protecting the authenticated browser request does not by itself address misuse of the application's own network requests; both attack surfaces need attention.
source_section: Introduction
source_passage:
A [Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)](https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/v42/4-Web_Application_Security_Testing/06-Session_Management_Testing/05-Testing_for_Cross_Site_Request_Forgery) attack occurs when a malicious web site, email, blog, instant message, or program tricks an authenticated user's web browser into performing an unwanted action on a trusted site. If a target user is authenticated to the site, unprotected target sites cannot distinguish between legitimate authorized requests and forged authenticated requests.

Since browser requests automatically include all cookies including session cookies, this attack works unless proper authorization is used, which means that the target site's challenge-response mechanism does not verify the identity and authority of the requester. In effect, CSRF attacks make a target system perform attacker-specified functions via the victim's browser without the victim's knowledge (normally until after the unauthorized actions have been committed).

extra_sources.source_section: Context
extra_sources.source_passage:
SSRF is an attack vector that abuses an application to interact with the internal/external network or the machine itself. One of the enablers for this vector is the mishandling of URLs, as showcased in the following examples:

- Image on an external server (*e.g.* user enters image URL of their avatar for the application to download and use).
- Custom [WebHook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Webhook) (users have to specify Webhook handlers or Callback URLs).
- Internal requests to interact with another service to serve a specific functionality. Most of the times, user data is sent along to be processed, and if poorly handled, can perform specific injection attacks.

question: we're on AWS EC2 -- is there a specific mitigation against SSRF being abused to steal instance credentials from the metadata service?
answer: Yes -- migrate to IMDSv2 and disable the old IMDSv1. IMDSv2 is a defense-in-depth mechanism for AWS that mitigates some instances of SSRF being used to access and steal credentials and access tokens from the instance metadata service.
source_section: IMDSv2 in AWS
source_passage:
In cloud environments SSRF is often used to access and steal credentials and access tokens from metadata services (e.g. AWS Instance Metadata Service, Azure Instance Metadata Service, GCP metadata server).

[IMDSv2](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/defense-in-depth-open-firewalls-reverse-proxies-ssrf-vulnerabilities-ec2-instance-metadata-service/) is an additional defense-in-depth mechanism for AWS that mitigates some of the instances of SSRF.

To leverage this protection migrate to IMDSv2 and disable old IMDSv1.

question: our webhook feature lets customers register a callback URL that our server later POSTs to -- since we can't allowlist arbitrary customer URLs ahead of time, what step-by-step validation should happen before that outbound request actually fires?
answer: Reject the request unless every one of these checks passes: (1) validate that the supplied value is a well-formed IP address or domain name; (2) apply a block-list check -- for an IP, verify it's a public address; for a domain, verify it resolves as public (not via an internal-only resolver) and then re-validate every A/AAAA address it resolves to as public, binding the connection to that validated address; (3) validate the requested protocol against an allowlist of HTTP/HTTPS only; (4) validate the token parameter name against a strict character set; (5) validate the token value against a strict character set; (6) validate any other business data needed for the call; then (7) build the HTTP POST request using only that validated information, connect only to the IP address already validated in step 2, and disable redirect-following in the HTTP client.
source_section: Cases > Case 2 - Application can send requests to ANY external IP address or domain name > Available protections > Application layer
source_passage:
**Validation flow (if one the validation steps fail then the request is rejected):**

1. The application will receive the IP address or domain name of the *TargetedApplication* and it will apply the first validation on the input data using the libraries/regex mentioned in this [section](Server_Side_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.md#application-layer).
2. The second validation will be applied against the IP address or domain name of the *TargetedApplication* using the following block-list approach:
   - For IP address:
     - The application will verify that it is a public one (see the hint provided in the next paragraph with the python code sample).
   - For domain name:
        1. The application will verify that it is a public one by trying to resolve the domain name against the DNS resolver that will only resolve internal domain name. Here, it must return a response indicating that it do not know the provided domain because the expected value received must be a public domain.
        2. Retrieve all the IP addresses behind the domain name (records *A* + *AAAA* for IPv4 + IPv6) and apply the same public-address verification described above. Bind the connection to a validated address as described under [domain name validation](#domain-name); checking DNS answers separately does not prevent DNS rebinding.
3. The application will receive the protocol to use for the request via a dedicated input parameter for which it will verify the value against an allowed list of protocols (`HTTP` or `HTTPS`).
4. The application will receive the parameter name for the token to pass to the *TargetedApplication* via a dedicated input parameter for which it will only allow the characters set `[a-z]{1,10}`.
5. The application will receive the token itself via a dedicated input parameter for which it will only allow the characters set `[a-zA-Z0-9]{20}`.
6. The application will receive and validate (from a security point of view) any business data needed to perform a valid call.
7. The application will build the HTTP POST request **using only validated information** and connect only to an IP address validated in step 2 (*don't forget to disable the support for [redirection](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Redirections) in the web client used*).

question: my server shells out to curl with a user-supplied URL to fetch remote content, and I pass the URL as its own argument via ProcessBuilder so it can't break out into other shell commands -- is that enough, or is there another whole class of attack I still need to handle?
answer: No. Passing one argument through a process API avoids shell interpolation, but the OS Command Injection sheet also says to pass exactly one validated URL, use `--globoff`, and remember that `--` alone does not prevent additional curl transfers. Argument separation does not validate the destination. Where the application's intended targets are known, the SSRF sheet says to allowlist the host or IP/domain, build the request from that accepted target with fixed scheme, port, and path, and avoid forwarding unchecked URL components.
source_section: Primary Defenses > Defense option 3: Parameterization in conjunction with Input Validation > Layer 2
source_passage: For commands that support it, use `--` to end option parsing. In [curl](https://curl.se/docs/manpage.html#OPTIONS), later arguments are still URL operands: `--` does not prevent additional transfers. Pass exactly one validated URL as one argument using a process API, and disable curl's [URL globbing](https://curl.se/docs/manpage.html#GLOBBING) with `--globoff`. Do not interpolate an unquoted value into a shell command. Argument separation does not validate the destination; apply [SSRF protections](Server_Side_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.md).

extra_sources.source_section: Cases > Case 1 - Application can send request only to identified and trusted applications > Available protections > Application layer > URL
extra_sources.source_passage: **Match the host against an allowlist, and build the request yourself.** The input here is an IP address or a domain name rather than a whole URL, so compare that value against an explicit [allowlist](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Input_Validation_Cheat_Sheet.html#allowlist-vs-denylist) of permitted destinations, then build the request from the entry that matched, together with a scheme, port and path the application fixes itself. Where that host was extracted from a URL the user supplied, do not copy the other components of that URL across either: carrying its path or query through, rather than rebuilding them, hands the next component something it has to parse again.

question: We're planning to let users upload custom email templates that might use Jinja2 or Twig. The cheat sheet has a table of engine-specific restrictions for this case — what should we set Jinja2's environment to, and what Twig function must never be allowed even inside a sandbox?
answer: For Jinja2, use SandboxedEnvironment (or ImmutableSandboxedEnvironment if you also need to block changes to lists, sets, and dictionaries). For Twig, never allow the template_from_string() function in sandboxed templates.
source_section: Engine Configuration
source_passage:
| Engine | Restrictions for untrusted templates |
| --- | --- |
| Jinja2 | Use [`SandboxedEnvironment`](https://jinja.palletsprojects.com/en/stable/sandbox/), or `ImmutableSandboxedEnvironment` to also block changes to lists, sets, and dictionaries. Restrict attributes further by overriding `is_safe_attribute()`, and decorate dangerous methods with `unsafe()`. |
| Twig | Twig treats templates as trusted code, so its [sandbox](https://twig.symfony.com/doc/3.x/sandbox.html) is the only boundary for untrusted authors. Give the sandbox its own environment and a strict `SecurityPolicy` that allowlists the tags, filters, functions, tests, methods, and properties templates may use. The `Sandbox` class requires Twig 3.29 or later. Never allow [`template_from_string()`](https://twig.symfony.com/doc/3.x/functions/template_from_string.html) in sandboxed templates. |
| FreeMarker | Follow the [FAQ on uploaded templates](https://freemarker.apache.org/docs/app_faq.html#faq_template_uploading_security): set the `?new` class resolver to `ALLOWS_NOTHING_RESOLVER`, not `SAFER_RESOLVER`; keep `?api` disabled (the default), restrict member access with `SimpleObjectWrapper` or a `WhitelistMemberAccessPolicy`, disable DOM node wrapping, and use a template loader that only loads approved files. |

question: Deserialization bugs and XXE both come from parsing data an attacker controls. Is one of them capped at information disclosure while the other can get an attacker to full RCE?
answer: No. The deserialization sheet lists denial of service, access-control attacks, and remote code execution as possible consequences. The XXE sheet lists local-file exposure, SSRF, and resource exhaustion. Those passages describe different documented effects; they do not establish an absolute ceiling on what every XXE exploit can achieve.
source_section: What is Deserialization
source_passage: Attacks against deserializers have been found to allow denial-of-service, access control, or remote code execution (RCE) attacks.

extra_sources.source_section: Introduction
extra_sources.source_passage: XML External Entity (XXE) injection occurs when an XML processor resolves an external entity from untrusted input. This can expose local files, cause server-side request forgery (SSRF), or exhaust resources.

review_notes: Corrected the false implication in the question and original answer that XXE is capped at information disclosure; the cited XXE passage also names SSRF and resource exhaustion.

question: We want to harden Java's ObjectInputStream by overriding resolveClass() so only our own Bicycle class can ever be deserialized. What should that override actually do with anything else that comes through?

If they differ, it throws `new InvalidClassException("Unauthorized deserialization attempt", desc.getName())`; only the matching class reaches `super.resolveClass(desc)`. The cheat sheet labels this an illustrative class check, not a complete deserialization defense.

question: Say our parser needs DTD support for a legacy integration, and while locking down external entities we find one hardening setting isn't supported by our parser version. What does the cheat sheet say we should do in that case?

question: What's the actual fix for mass assignment — is it enough to just blocklist a sensitive field like 'isAdmin', or what's the recommended approach?
answer: Blocklisting a specific field like isAdmin is not the recommended approach, because a new or overlooked sensitive field stays bindable. Instead, prefer dedicated input objects (DTOs) that only contain the fields a caller may edit, and explicitly allow-list which fields can be bound when binding to an object that has additional properties.
source_section: Introduction > Solutions
source_passage:
- Prefer dedicated input objects, such as Data Transfer Objects (DTOs), containing only fields the caller may edit; see [Spring's model design guidance](https://docs.spring.io/spring-framework/reference/web/webmvc/mvc-data-binding.html).
- Explicitly allow-list fields when binding to an object with additional properties.
- Do not rely on a block-list as the sole protection: a new or overlooked sensitive field remains bindable. [CWE-915 recommends allowlists over denylists](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/915.html). The block-list examples below illustrate mechanisms encountered in existing applications, not the recommended design.

question: Our pen test report flagged both an IDOR and a mass assignment finding on the same /update_profile endpoint and called them 'the same root cause.' Is that actually accurate?
answer: Not quite — they're related access-control gaps but not identical. IDOR means the app is missing an object-level authorization check: a user supplies a reference (ID, UUID, token, etc.) to an object and the app never verifies they're allowed to access or manipulate that specific object. Mass assignment is a different mechanism: a framework auto-binds incoming request parameters straight into an object's fields, so an attacker can set fields they were never meant to control (like isAdmin) even on an object they ARE authorized to update.
source_section: Introduction
source_passage:
There are three ingredients to an IDOR:

1. An **object** such as an account, document, support ticket, transaction or partner profile.
2. A **reference** to that object in the form of an ID, UUID, account number, token or slug.
3. A **missing object-level authorization check** that allows a user to access or manipulate an object they should not be able to access.

extra_sources.source_section: Introduction > Definition
extra_sources.source_passage:
Software frameworks sometimes allow developers to automatically bind HTTP request parameters into program code variables or objects to make using that framework easier on developers. This can sometimes cause harm.

Attackers can sometimes use this methodology to create new parameters that the developer never intended which in turn creates or overwrites new variable or objects in program code that was not intended.

This is called a **Mass Assignment** vulnerability.

question: Before we ship this feature, how should we actually test that object-level access control is enforced everywhere, instead of just eyeballing the code?
answer: Create two test user accounts (User A and User B), create objects owned by each one (documents, support tickets, invoices, etc.), then authenticate as User A and try to access User B's objects by modifying the object references in requests. Verify access is denied regardless of whether the identifier is predictable or hard to guess.
source_section: Verifying access controls
source_passage:
1. Create User A and User B.
2. Create objects owned by each user (documents, support tickets, invoices, etc.).
3. Authenticate as User A and attempt to access User B's objects by modifying object references in requests.
4. Verify that the application denies unauthorized access regardless of whether the object identifier is predictable or unguessable.

question: If we're stuck using an object literal somewhere and can't switch to Map/Set or Object.create(null), what fallback does this cheat sheet suggest, and how seriously does it treat that option?
answer: As a last resort, you can set the __proto__ property directly in the literal (e.g. {__proto__: null}) to stop it inheriting from Object.prototype — but it's explicitly framed as a last resort, not a first choice.
source_section: Suggested protection mechanisms > If objects or object literals are required
source_passage:
If objects have to be used then they should be created using the `Object.create(null)` API to ensure they don't inherit from the Object prototype:

```javascript
let obj = Object.create(null);
```

If object literals are required then as a last resort you could use the `__proto__` property:

```javascript
let obj = {__proto__:null};
```
review_notes: Expanded the passage to include the null-prototype explanation and the actual object-literal example supporting the answer.

question: We just decommissioned an old promo microsite at promo.ourapp.com (it was hosted on Heroku) but haven't removed the DNS record yet, and our clickjacking defense uses a CSP like frame-ancestors 'self' https://*.ourapp.com. Should we be worried about that combination?
answer: Yes. The sheet illustrates how a leftover CNAME to a deleted Heroku app can become claimable by an attacker. If they take control of `promo.ourapp.com`, the wildcard `https://*.ourapp.com` in `frame-ancestors` includes that HTTPS subdomain, so it could frame the protected site. During decommissioning, update or remove the DNS record, wait for propagation, and then remove the cloud resource; specify only trusted framing origins rather than trusting all subdomains.
source_section: Introduction
source_passage: - **Bypass Content Security Policy** rules that trust wildcard subdomains (`*.example.com`)

extra_sources.source_section: Subdomain Takeover Prevention Cheat Sheet > How Subdomain Takeover Works > The Basic Mechanism
extra_sources.source_passage:
1. An organization creates a DNS record: `blog.example.com CNAME example-blog.herokuapp.com`
2. The Heroku app serves content on `blog.example.com`
3. Months later, the team decommissions the Heroku app but forgets to remove the DNS record
4. The CNAME still points to `example-blog.herokuapp.com`, which no longer exists
5. An attacker creates a new Heroku app with the name `example-blog` and claims the hostname
6. The attacker now controls what is served on `blog.example.com`

extra_sources.source_section: Defending with Content Security Policy (CSP) frame-ancestors directive > Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors Examples
extra_sources.source_passage:
- `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self' https://*.somesite.com https://myfriend.site.com;`
    - For an HTTPS page, this allows its own origin, HTTPS subdomains of `somesite.com`, and `https://myfriend.site.com` to frame it. The two HTTPS host expressions use the default port (443). The [wildcard matches subdomains](https://www.w3.org/TR/CSP3/#match-hosts), not the bare `somesite.com` host; add that host explicitly if required.

extra_sources.source_section: Subdomain Takeover Prevention Cheat Sheet > Prevention Strategies > 1. Manage DNS Record Lifecycle During Decommissioning
extra_sources.source_passage:
The correct order of operations when decommissioning a service is:

1. **Redirect or serve a maintenance page** at the subdomain to avoid broken links and user confusion during the transition period
2. **Update or remove the DNS record** pointing to the resource
3. **Wait for DNS propagation** (at least the TTL duration, typically 300 to 3600 seconds)
4. **Then decommission the cloud resource**

review_notes: Added the Heroku dangling-DNS mechanism and decommissioning-order evidence; described takeover as a possibility subject to claimability rather than a certainty.

question: What idle timeout should I use for a banking app versus some low-risk internal tool?
answer: For high-value applications like banking, use a short idle timeout of about 2-5 minutes; for low-risk applications, 15-30 minutes is acceptable. Absolute timeouts are set separately based on expected usage duration -- e.g. 4-8 hours for an app used by an office worker all day.

question: What do I actually need to do in code when a user's privilege level changes mid-session, like right after they log in or get promoted to admin?
answer: Regenerate/renew the session ID rather than reusing it whenever a privilege level change occurs (login, password change, role elevation, etc.): only the new session ID should be accepted on subsequent requests for protected resources, and the old one must be destroyed. Frameworks provide calls for this, such as `session_regenerate_id(true)` in PHP, `request.getSession(true)`/`HttpSession.invalidate()` in J2EE, or `Session.Abandon()` in ASP .NET.
source_section: Session Management Cheat Sheet > Session ID Life Cycle > Renew the Session ID After Any Privilege Level Change
source_passage:
The session ID must be renewed or regenerated by the web application after any privilege level change within the associated user session. The most common scenario where the session ID regeneration is mandatory is during the authentication process, as the privilege level of the user changes from the unauthenticated (or anonymous) state to the authenticated state though in some cases still not yet the authorized state. Common scenarios to consider include; password changes, permission changes, or switching from a regular user role to an administrator role within the web application. For all sensitive pages of the web application, any previous session IDs must be ignored, only the current session ID must be assigned to every new request received for the protected resource, and the old or previous session ID must be destroyed.

The most common web development frameworks provide session functions and methods to renew the session ID, such as `request.getSession(true)` & `HttpSession.invalidate()` (J2EE), `Session.Abandon()` & `Response.Cookies.Add(new...)` (ASP .NET), or `session_start()` & `session_regenerate_id(true)` (PHP).

question: I've got two separate worries: someone cracking stored password hashes, and someone hijacking a session via a predictable or fixated session ID. Is that the same OWASP guidance, or do I need to look in two different places?
answer: They are covered by different sheets. The Password Storage Cheat Sheet addresses offline password guessing by recommending slow password hashes such as Argon2id, bcrypt, or PBKDF2 with unique salts, rather than plaintext or fast SHA-256. The Session Management Cheat Sheet identifies disclosure, capture, prediction, brute force, and fixation of a session ID as paths to session hijacking. One concerns stored credentials; the other concerns an active authenticated session.
source_section: Password Storage Cheat Sheet > Introduction
source_passage: Passwords should never be stored in plain text. Instead, they must be protected using strong, slow hashing algorithms such as Argon2id, bcrypt, or PBKDF2. A unique salt must be added to each password to prevent attackers from using precomputed lookup tables like rainbow tables. Fast hashing algorithms such as SHA‑256 are not suitable for password storage because they allow attackers to perform large numbers of guesses quickly.

extra_sources.source_section: Session Management Cheat Sheet > Introduction
extra_sources.source_passage: The disclosure, capture, prediction, brute force, or fixation of the session ID will lead to session hijacking (or sidejacking) attacks, where an attacker is able to fully impersonate a victim user in the web application.

review_notes: Removed session-ID generation and regeneration advice that was not in the cited Session Management introduction.

question: What's the lowest-memory Argon2id setting OWASP still considers acceptable if I'm tight on RAM?
answer: The lowest-memory configuration listed is m=7168 (7 MiB), t=5, p=1. All five listed configurations (46/19/12/9/7 MiB paired with t=1 through t=5 respectively) provide an equivalent level of defense -- the only trade-off is between CPU time and RAM usage.
source_section: Password Storage Cheat Sheet > Password Hashing Algorithms > Argon2id
source_passage:
Tune memory and iteration costs to make password cracking expensive while keeping authentication practical under expected load. [Benchmark the chosen parameters on the target system](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9106.html#section-4); increasing parallelism is not a guarantee of slower password guessing. Use one of the following minimum configurations:

- m=47104 (46 MiB), t=1, p=1 (Do not use with Argon2i)
- m=19456 (19 MiB), t=2, p=1 (Do not use with Argon2i)
- m=12288 (12 MiB), t=3, p=1
- m=9216 (9 MiB), t=4, p=1
- m=7168 (7 MiB), t=5, p=1

These configuration settings provide an equal level of defense, and the only difference is a trade off between CPU and RAM usage.

question: Why do people keep saying I need PKCE even for my backend web app, not just mobile apps?
answer: Because current OAuth 2.0 best practice requires PKCE with the Authorization Code Grant for all client types -- not just native/mobile apps -- including single-page apps and other clients. The Implicit Grant is deprecated, and PKCE is what protects the Authorization Code Grant against authorization code interception regardless of client type.
source_section: OAuth 2.0 Protocol Cheatsheet > Implicit Grant (DEPRECATED — DO NOT USE)
source_passage: Clients **must** use the Authorization Code Grant with PKCE (`response_type=code`) for all client types, including SPAs and native applications.

question: What should I actually do to stop a stolen refresh token from being reused by an attacker?
answer: Either sender-constrain the refresh token (bind it to the client using DPoP or mTLS, so a stolen token can't be used without the matching private key) or implement refresh token rotation -- issue a new refresh token on every use and immediately invalidate the old one so reuse of a stolen token is detectable. Combining both approaches provides defense-in-depth.
source_section: OAuth 2.0 Protocol Cheatsheet > Token Replay Prevention > When to Use PoP Tokens
source_passage: Refresh tokens are sender-constrained (using DPoP or mTLS) or use refresh token rotation (issuing new refresh tokens and invalidating old ones immediately to detect replay attempts). **Note:** Combining PoP-constrained refresh tokens with rotation provides defense-in-depth.
review_notes: Corrected the full section path for the cited refresh-token sentence, which lies under the When to Use PoP Tokens subsection.

question: What's the baseline transport protection I need for SAML messages flowing between my IdP and SP?
answer: At minimum, use TLS 1.2, the most common solution cited for protecting SAML message confidentiality and integrity at the transport layer; this helps counter eavesdropping, theft of authentication information/bearer tokens, message deletion/modification, and man-in-the-middle attacks.
source_section: SAML Security Cheat Sheet > Validate Message Confidentiality and Integrity
source_passage:
[TLS 1.2](Transport_Layer_Security_Cheat_Sheet.md) is the most common solution to guarantee message confidentiality and integrity at the transport layer. Refer to [SAML Security (section 4.2.1)](https://docs.oasis-open.org/security/saml/v2.0/saml-sec-consider-2.0-os.pdf) for additional information. This step will help counter the following attacks:

- Theft of User Authentication Information 7.1.1.2
- Theft of the Bearer Token 7.1.1.3
- Message Deletion 7.1.1.6

question: What concrete steps should my SAML Service Provider take to avoid signature-wrapping attacks when validating an IdP's response?
answer: Obtain the IdP's signing key(s) out of band rather than trusting any embedded KeyInfo element: use a StaticKeySelector when you expect a single signing key, or an X509KeySelector/JKS variant when you expect more than one, storing the keys locally either way. To avoid XML signature-wrapping attacks specifically, never use `getElementsByTagName` to select security-related elements without prior validation, and always use absolute XPath expressions to select elements (unless a hardened schema is used for validation).
source_section: SAML Security Cheat Sheet > Validate Protocol Usage > Validate Signatures
source_passage:
- If you expect only one signing key, use `StaticKeySelector`. Obtain the key directly from the identity provider, store it in a local file and ignore any `KeyInfo` elements in the document.
- If you expect more than one signing key, use `X509KeySelector` (the JKS variant). Obtain these keys directly from the identity providers, store them in local JKS and ignore any `KeyInfo` elements in the document.
- Avoid signature-wrapping attacks.
    - Never use `getElementsByTagName` to select security related elements in an XML document without prior validation.
    - Always use absolute XPath expressions to select elements, unless a hardened schema is used for validation.

question: My team wants to 'just use JWTs for SSO instead of dealing with OAuth or SAML' -- is that actually a like-for-like swap?
answer: No. JWT describes a token carrying claims that can be signed and/or encrypted. It is used inside other systems: OpenID Connect's ID token is a JWT, and an OAuth 2 access token can be a JWT. The OAuth sheet describes OAuth as a basis for federated login and OpenID Connect as its identity layer; the SAML sheet describes exchanging authentication and authorization information and a browser SSO profile. Choosing JWT as a token does not replace those login and federation mechanisms.
source_section: JSON Web Token Cheat Sheet > Introduction
source_passage:
[**JSON Web Tokens**](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7519) (JWT) are security tokens for carrying information (**claims**), often about a user, an application, etc. (**subject**). JWTs can provide authenticity of the claims (**signed JWT**) and/or confidentiality of the claims (**encrypted JWT**). In addition, JWT defines [standard claims](https://www.iana.org/assignments/jwt/jwt.xhtml).

JWTs are used in a wide range of applications such as:

- In [OpenID Connect](https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-core-1_0.html), the [ID token](https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-core-1_0.html#IDToken) is a JWT used to represent the identity and attributes of the connected user.
- In [OAuth 2](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6749), the access token used to obtain access to a protected resource [can be a JWT](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9068).

extra_sources.source_section: OAuth 2.0 Protocol Cheatsheet
extra_sources.source_passage: This cheatsheet describes the best current security practices for [OAuth 2.0](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6749.html) as derived from its RFC. OAuth became the standard for API protection and the basis for federated login using OpenID Connect. OpenID Connect 1.0 is a simple identity layer on top of the OAuth 2.0 protocol. It enables clients to verify the identity of the end user based on the authentication performed by an authorization server, as well as to obtain basic profile information about the end user in an interoperable and REST-like manner.

extra_sources.source_section: SAML Security Cheat Sheet > Introduction
extra_sources.source_passage: The **S**ecurity **A**ssertion **M**arkup **L**anguage ([SAML](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Security_Assertion_Markup_Language)) is an open standard for exchanging authorization and authentication information. The *Web Browser SAML/SSO Profile with Redirect/POST bindings* is one of the most common SSO implementation. This cheatsheet will focus primarily on that profile.

question: If I decide to use a JWT as my session token, what do I actually need to nail down about expiration so I don't end up with sessions I can't kill early?
answer: Plan session invalidation separately from expiration. The JWT sheet gives a denylist of revoked sessions/tokens as one solution, while noting that it makes sessions no longer completely stateless. The Session Management sheet requires an idle timeout and an absolute timeout regardless of activity, with expiration enforced server-side. At the absolute limit, invalidate the session and require re-authentication. JWT-based sessions still need those expiration and invalidation controls.
source_section: JSON Web Token Cheat Sheet > Considerations about using JWTs > Not using JWTs
source_passage: JWTs are often suggested for “stateless” user sessions. However, if you use JWTs for user sessions, you will need a solution for managing session invalidation. This can be achieved using a deny list of revoked sessions/tokens. If your application implements such a deny list, user sessions won't be completely stateless anymore which might defeat the benefits of stateless sessions.

extra_sources.source_section: Session Management Cheat Sheet > Session Expiration > Automatic Session Expiration > Absolute Timeout
extra_sources.source_passage: All sessions should implement an absolute timeout, regardless of session activity. This timeout defines the maximum amount of time a session can be active, closing and invalidating the session upon the defined absolute period since the given session was initially created by the web application. After invalidating the session, the user is forced to (re)authenticate again in the web application and establish a new session.

extra_sources.source_section: Session Management Cheat Sheet > Session Expiration > Automatic Session Expiration > Idle Timeout
extra_sources.source_passage:
All sessions should implement an idle or inactivity timeout. This timeout defines the amount of time a session will remain active in case there is no activity in the session, closing and invalidating the session upon the defined idle period since the last HTTP request received by the web application for a given session ID.

The idle timeout limits the chances an attacker has to guess and use a valid session ID from another user. However, if the attacker is able to hijack a given session, the idle timeout does not limit the attacker's actions, as they can generate activity on the session periodically to keep the session active for longer periods of time.

Session timeout management and expiration must be enforced server-side. If the client is used to enforce the session timeout, for example using the session token or other client parameters to track time references (e.g. number of minutes since login time), an attacker could manipulate these to extend the session duration.

review_notes: Removed unsupported short-exp/refresh prescriptions and the claim that a denylist is the only invalidation solution; expanded session evidence to cover re-authentication and server-side idle expiration.

question: If my access-control logic hits some edge case it wasn't designed for, should the app lean toward letting the request through or blocking it?
answer: Block it. The application should always default to denying access when no rule explicitly grants it ('deny by default'), rather than leaning permissive for unmatched or unanticipated cases.
source_section: Authorization Cheat Sheet > Recommendations > Deny by Default
source_passage: Even when no access control rules are explicitly matched, the application cannot remain neutral when an entity is requesting access to a particular resource. The application must always make a decision, whether implicitly or explicitly, to either deny or permit the requested access. Logic errors and other mistakes relating to access control may happen, especially when access requirements are complex; consequently, one should not rely entirely on explicitly defined rules for matching all possible requests. For security purposes an application should be configured to deny access by default.

question: I've added permission checks to most of my API's controller methods one by one -- is that a solid way to enforce authorization?
answer: No -- relying on manually adding checks method-by-method is risky because an attacker only needs to find the one place you missed, and even a single missed check can jeopardize a resource. Instead use a global, application-wide enforcement mechanism (such as a servlet filter, framework middleware, or an interceptor) so permissions are validated consistently on every request, rather than depending on per-method diligence.
source_section: Authorization Cheat Sheet > Recommendations > Validate the Permissions on Every Request
source_passage: Permission should be validated correctly on every request, regardless of whether the request was initiated by an AJAX script, server-side, or any other source. The technology used to perform such checks should allow for global, application-wide configuration rather than needing to be applied individually to every method or class. Remember an attacker only needs to find one way in. Even if just a single access control check is "missed", the confidentiality and/or integrity of a resource can be jeopardized.

question: When I build password-reset tokens, do the security rules basically mirror what I'd do for stored passwords, or is there something different about handling a reset token?
answer: They share the need for secure storage, but the cited guidance does not prescribe the same hashing method for both. Passwords should be stored using strong, slow hashes with a unique salt. Password-reset tokens should be generated with a cryptographically safe random generator, be long enough to resist brute force, be stored securely, and additionally be single-use and expire after an appropriate period.
source_section: Forgot Password Cheat Sheet > Introduction
source_passage:
- **Ensure that generated tokens or codes are:**
    - **Randomly generated using a cryptographically safe algorithm.**
    - **Sufficiently long to protect against brute-force attacks.**
    - **Stored securely.**
    - **Single use and expire after an appropriate period.**

A unique salt must be added to each password to prevent attackers from using precomputed lookup tables like rainbow tables.

question: What's a safe way to use security questions in a 'forgot password' flow without letting attackers figure out which emails are registered?
answer: Don't show the security question until after the user has proven ownership of the email address. Have them submit their email (with a CAPTCHA), always show a generic message like 'if that email is correct, an email will be sent to it', email a single-use random link, and only present the security question(s) after they click that link. Asking the question up front -- before verifying the email -- would let an attacker enumerate which addresses have accounts. After a correct answer to the security question(s), allow the user to enter a new password.
source_section: Choosing and Using Security Questions Cheat Sheet > Using Security Questions > When to Use Security Questions > Forgotten Password or Lost MFA Token Flow
source_passage:
Forgotten password functionality often provides a mechanism for attackers to enumerate user accounts if it is not correctly implemented. The following flow avoids this issue by only displaying the security questions once the user has proved ownership of the email address:

- The user enters email address (and solves a CAPTCHA).
- The application displays a generic message such as "If the email address was correct, an email will be sent to it".
- An email with a randomly generated, single-use link is sent to the user.
- The user clicks the link.
- The user is presented with the security question(s).
- If the answer is correct, the user can enter a new password.
review_notes: Included the introductory explanation supporting the enumeration claim and completed the flow with successful answer verification before setting a new password.

question: What's the technical difference between 'primary authentication' and what the patterns cheat sheet calls 'authentication proof verification'?
answer: Primary authentication is the one-time act of verifying an actual credential (a password, a WebAuthn assertion, a machine certificate, a workload identity like a SPIFFE ID) and binding it to a known identity. Authentication proof verification is the repeated, lighter-weight check of the reusable artifact issued afterward -- a session cookie, token, or assertion at the application layer, or a TLS session key or IPsec Security Association at lower layers -- so that primary authentication doesn't have to be repeated on every request.
source_section: Authentication Patterns Cheat Sheet > Introduction
source_passage:
- **Primary authentication** verifies a credential and links it to a known identity: a password, a signed challenge such as a [WebAuthn assertion](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Web_Authentication_API), or, for internal actors, a machine certificate or a workload identity such as a [SPIFFE ID](https://spiffe.io/docs/latest/spiffe-about/overview/).
- **Authentication proof verification** checks the reusable artifact issued after primary authentication (a session cookie, token, or assertion at the application layer; a TLS session key or IPsec Security Association at lower layers) so that primary authentication is not repeated on every request.

question: How can I run a Docker container with an unprivileged user or map container root to an unprivileged host user?
answer: Three options: (1) at runtime, pass the -u option to docker run (e.g. docker run -u 4000 alpine); (2) at build time, add a dedicated user in the Dockerfile with groupadd/useradd and then a USER directive before the app runs; or (3) enable user namespace remapping (--userns-remap=default) in the Docker daemon so container root maps to an unprivileged host user.
source_section: Docker Security Cheat Sheet > Rules > RULE #2 - Set a user
source_passage:
Configuring the container to use an unprivileged user is the best way to prevent privilege escalation attacks. This can be accomplished in three different ways as follows:

1. During runtime using `-u` option of `docker run` command e.g.:

```bash
docker run -u 4000 alpine
```

2. During build time. Simply add user in Dockerfile and use it. For example:

```dockerfile
FROM alpine
RUN groupadd -r myuser && useradd -r -g myuser myuser
#    <HERE DO WHAT YOU HAVE TO DO AS A ROOT USER LIKE INSTALLING PACKAGES ETC.>
USER myuser
```

3. Enable user namespace support (`--userns-remap=default`) in [Docker daemon](https://docs.docker.com/engine/security/userns-remap/#enable-userns-remap-on-the-daemon)
review_notes: Distinguished a non-root container user from user namespace remapping, which limits host privileges without necessarily changing container UID 0. Kept the source example unchanged; its Alpine groupadd/useradd commands may require additional packages.

question: Docker Secrets seem like a solid way to handle sensitive data in containers — can I rely on the same approach once those containers are running under Kubernetes instead of plain Docker?
answer: The Docker sheet says not to assume the same approach applies to Kubernetes. It describes Docker Swarm Secrets as distributed over mutual TLS and stored in an encrypted Raft log, while warning that Kubernetes Secrets are stored without encryption by default. The Kubernetes sheet makes the at-rest distinction explicit: configure a non-`identity` encryption provider first for Secrets, then rewrite existing Secrets to encrypt previously stored data. The Docker sheet also suggests third-party tools.
source_section: Docker Security Cheat Sheet > Rules > RULE #12 - Utilize Docker Secrets for Sensitive Data Management
source_passage:
Docker Secrets provide a secure way to store and manage sensitive data such as passwords, tokens, and SSH keys. Using Docker Secrets helps in avoiding the exposure of sensitive data in container images or in runtime commands.

```bash
docker secret create my_secret /path/to/super-secret-data.txt
docker service create --name web --secret my_secret nginx:latest
```

For local Docker Compose, [file-backed secrets are bind mounts](https://docs.docker.com/compose/how-tos/use-secrets/#use-secrets). Protect the source files on the host with appropriate access permissions and storage encryption; declaring a Compose secret does not encrypt these files. This differs from [Swarm-managed secrets](https://docs.docker.com/engine/swarm/secrets/#how-docker-manages-secrets), which are distributed over mutual TLS and stored in an encrypted Raft log:

```yaml
version: "3.8"
secrets:
  my_secret:
    file: ./super-secret-data.txt
services:
  web:
    image: nginx:latest
    secrets:
      - my_secret
```

While Docker Secrets generally provide a secure way to manage sensitive data in Docker environments, this approach is not recommended for Kubernetes, where secrets are stored in plaintext by default. In Kubernetes, consider using additional security measures such as etcd encryption, or third-party tools. Refer to the [Secrets Management Cheat Sheet](Secrets_Management_Cheat_Sheet.md) and [Kubernetes Security Cheat Sheet](Kubernetes_Security_Cheat_Sheet.md) for more information.

extra_sources.source_section: Kubernetes Security Cheat Sheet > Kubernetes Security Best Practices: Deploy Phase > Securing data > Encrypt secrets at rest
extra_sources.source_passage: Kubernetes [supports encryption at rest](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/encrypt-data/) for Secret resources in etcd, but the API server stores resources without at-rest encryption by default. Configure a non-`identity` encryption provider as the first provider for Secrets and [rewrite existing Secrets](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/encrypt-data/#ensure-all-secrets-are-encrypted) to encrypt previously stored data.

question: Why is everyone so paranoid about locking down etcd access in a Kubernetes cluster specifically?
answer: Because etcd stores all cluster state and secrets: write access to the API server's etcd is equivalent to gaining root on the entire cluster, and even read-only access can be used to escalate privileges fairly easily.

Write access to the API server's etcd is equivalent to gaining root on the entire cluster, and even read access can be used to escalate privileges fairly easily.

question: We generate a signed SBOM for every release now. Does that by itself give us enough to actually trust a release, or is there more we need from the broader supply-chain-security side?
answer: No. The SBOM sheet says a valid signature authenticates claims and their integrity, but does not prove that the SBOM is accurate or complete, that the software is safe, or that the trusted builder was not compromised. The supply-chain sheet additionally calls for provenance generated by the build platform that is difficult to forge and detailed enough to link the release artifact back to its builder.

question: This cheat sheet buckets supply-chain threats into four broad categories. What are they?
answer: Source code threats, build environment threats, dependency-related threats, and deployment and runtime threats.
source_section: Software Supply Chain Security > Overview of Threat Landscape
source_passage:
- Source code threats. These type of threats focus on violating the integrity of a source code which is then built and and deployed or potentially consumed by other software projects. Threats in this category include VCS exploits, the introduction of malicious or vulnerable code into a codebase, or building code from an unauthorized branch.
- Build environment threats. These threats modify a software artifact but without altering the underlying source code or exploiting the build process itself. Examples include build cache poisoning, compromising a privileged account used by the build tool, or publishing software built from an untrusted source.
- Dependency related threats. Threats that result from the consumption of both direct and transitive software dependencies. The most common threat is using a vulnerable or compromised dependency.
- Deployment and runtime threats. These threats exploit either the deployment process or runtime environment. Common examples include compromising a privilege CI/CD account, software misconfigurations, and deployment of compromised binaries.

question: Before I pull in some open-source library for a project, what questions should I actually be asking to vet it from a security angle?
answer: Among others: Is the project actively maintained? Is it sufficiently popular/well-known in its community? Is it mature? Is the version you'd use an actual release (not alpha/beta)? Does it have enough maintainers/contributors for its complexity? Does it keep its own dependencies updated? Does it have solid test coverage including security-relevant tests? Is it well-documented, including secure-usage guidance? Does it have an established, documented vulnerability-reporting process with timely fixes? And is your intended use consistent with its license?
source_section: Software Supply Chain Security > Mitigations and Security Best Practices > Mitigating Dependency Threats > Assess Suppliers
source_passage:
- Is the project actively maintained?
- Is the project sufficiently popular and well-known in the applicable community?
- Is the project sufficiently mature?
- Is the product or version being evaluated a "release" version, e.g. not an alpha, beta, or comparable versions?
- Given the complexity of the project, does the project have a sufficient number of maintainers and contributors?
- Does the project keep its dependencies updated?
- Does the project have sufficient test coverage and do the tests include security relevant rules?
- Is the project well-documented and does the document include guidance on how to use the component securely?
- Does the project have an established and documented process for reporting vulnerabilities and are these vulnerabilities addressed in a timely manner?
- Is the intended usage of the project consistent with the project's license?

question: What's the actual harm in leaving some cloud resources untagged when we provision infrastructure via IaC?
answer: Untagged assets tend to turn into "ghost resources" that are hard to detect, visualize, or get observability into, which causes configuration drift in your security posture. They also quietly add to billing costs and make maintenance harder and reliability worse — the fix is careful tagging plus monitoring for untagged resources.
source_section: Infrastructure as Code Security Cheatsheet > Introduction > Deploy
source_passage: Tagging - It is essential to tag cloud assets properly. During IaC operations, untagged assets are most likely to result in ghost resources that make it difficult to detect, visualize, and gain observability within the cloud environment and can affect the posture causing a drift. These ghost resources can add to billing costs, make maintenance difficult, and affect the reliability. The only solution to this is careful tagging and monitoring for untagged resources.

question: Before any infrastructure actually gets deployed, what security steps should be built into the early 'write and share the IaC code' stage of the workflow?
answer: Use IDE security plugins (e.g. TFLint, Checkov) for early detection; build threat modeling into the dev cycle early; manage secrets properly instead of in plaintext files or committed to Git; keep IaC under version control with infrastructure changes checked in alongside the feature code they support (not separately); and apply least-privilege access policies that define exactly who is authorized to create, update, run, or delete the IaC scripts and inventory, and limit their permissions to only what's necessary.
source_section: Infrastructure as Code Security Cheatsheet > Introduction > Develop and Distribute
source_passage:
- IDE plugins - Leverage standard security plug-ins in the integrated development environment (IDE) which helps in the early detection of potential risks and drastically reduces the time to address any issues later in the development cycle. Plugins such as TFLint, Checkov, Docker Linter, docker-vulnerability-extension, Security Scan, Contrast Security, etc., help in the security assessment of the IaC.
- Threat modeling - Build the threat modeling landscape earlier in the development cycle to ensure there is enough visibility of the high-risk, high-volume aspects of the code and flexibility to include security throughout to ensure the assets are safely managed.
- Managing secrets -  Secrets are confidential data and information such as application tokens required for authentication, passwords, and SSH (Secure Shell) keys. The problem is not the secrets, but where you store them. If you are using a simple text file or SCMs like Git, then the secrets can be easily exposed. Open-source tools such as truffleHog, git-secrets, GitGuardian and similar can be utilized to detect such vulnerable management of secrets. See the [Secrets Management Cheat Sheet](Secrets_Management_Cheat_Sheet.md) for more information.
- Version control - Version control is the practice of tracking and managing changes to software code. Ensure all the changes to the IaC are tracked with the right set of information that helps in any revert operation. The important part is that you’re checking in those changes alongside the features they support and not separately. A feature’s infrastructure requirements should be a part of a feature’s branch or merge request. Git is generally used as the source code version control system.
- Principle of least privilege - define the access management policies based on the principle of least privilege with the following priority items:

    - Defining who is and is not authorized to create/update/run/delete the scripts and inventory.
    - Limiting the permissions of authorized IaC users to what is necessary to perform their tasks. The IaC scripts should ensure that the permissions granted to the various resources it creates are limited to what is required for them to perform their work.

question: NPM Security and Vulnerable Dependency Management both cover dependency vulnerabilities — what's actually different about what each one tells me to do?
answer: The NPM sheet describes continuous package vulnerability scanning and monitoring manifest snapshots for newly disclosed CVEs. The Vulnerable Dependency Management sheet organizes the response after an issue is detected into cases, including the case where the provider has already released a patched component. One emphasizes finding and monitoring package vulnerabilities; the other structures what the team does after finding one.
source_section: NPM Security best practices > 5) Audit for vulnerabilities in open source dependencies
source_passage:
Security doesn’t end by just scanning for security vulnerabilities when installing a package but should also be streamlined with developer workflows to be effectively adopted throughout the entire lifecycle of software development, and monitored continuously when code is deployed:

- Scan for security vulnerabilities in [third-party open source projects](https://owasp.org/www-community/Component_Analysis)
- Monitor snapshots of your project's manifests so you can receive alerts when new CVEs impact them [OWASP Dependency-Track](https://owasp.org/www-project-dependency-track/)

extra_sources.source_section: Vulnerable Dependency Management Cheat Sheet > Cases

When a security issue is detected, the development team can meet one of the situations (named _Case_ in the rest of the cheat sheet) presented in the sub sections below.

If the vulnerably impact a [transitive dependency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transitive_dependency) then the action will be taken on the direct dependency of the project because acting on a transitive dependency often impact the stability of the application.

Acting on a on a transitive dependency require the development team to fully understand the complete relation/communication/usage from the project first level dependency until the dependency impacted by the security vulnerability, this task is very time consuming.

### Case 1

#### Context

Patched version of the component has been released by the provider.

question: I've set ignore-scripts=true globally for npm, but the sharp package genuinely needs its install script to run. How do I allow just that one package via the lavamoat allow-scripts plugin, config-wise?
answer: Add a "lavamoat" key to package.json with an "allowScripts" object naming the package and setting it to true, e.g. {"lavamoat": {"allowScripts": {"sharp": true}}}.

question: Say a library maintainer flat-out refuses to fix a CVE in their package, or just never responds at all — what does this cheat sheet say to do?
answer: This is Case 3, a complex, time-consuming last resort in which the team may need to patch the dependency itself; an open-source fix can be contributed upstream. Study a better-maintained alternative in parallel, or, for a commercial component with support, involve the Chief Risk Officer (or CISO) to pressure the provider. Identify the dependency's use, examine the CVE and upstream advisory/issue/fix to establish the required change, and do not assume a generic wrapper fixes an unclear root cause. Verify the patch with a reproducer that fails before the patch and passes after it, keep dependency tests passing, and run available application tests for regressions. Suppress a scanner alert per CVE only after the patch is verified; changing a version string is not a fix.
source_section: Vulnerable Dependency Management Cheat Sheet > Cases > Case 3 > Context
source_passage:
Provider informs the team that they cannot fix the issue, so no patched version will be released at all (applies also if provider does not want to fix the issue or does not answer at all).

In this case the only information given to the development team is the [CVE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_Vulnerabilities_and_Exposures).

**Notes:**

- This case is really complex and time consuming and is generally used as last resort.
- If the impacted dependency is an open source library then we, the development team, can create a patch and create [pull request](https://help.github.com/en/articles/about-pull-requests) - that way we can protect our company/application from the source as well as helping others secure their applications.

extra_sources.source_section: Vulnerable Dependency Management Cheat Sheet > Cases > Case 3 > Approach
extra_sources.source_passage:
**Step 1:**

If we are in this case due to one of the following conditions, it's a good idea to start a parallel study to find another component better maintained or if it's a commercial component with support **then put pressure** on the provider with the help of your [Chief Risk Officer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_risk_officer) (fallback possible to [Chief Information Security Officer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_information_security_officer)):

- Provider does not want to fix the issue.
- Provider does not answer at all.

In all cases, here, we need to handle the vulnerability right now.

**Step 2:**

As we know the vulnerable dependency, we know where it is used in the application (if it's a transitive dependency then we can identify the first level dependency using it using the [IDE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integrated_development_environment) built-in feature or the dependency management system used (Maven, Gradle, NuGet, npm, etc.). Note that IDE is also used to identify the calls to the dependency.

Identifying calls to this dependency is fine but it is the first step. The team still lacks information on what kind of patching needs to be performed.

Use the CVE description to identify the reported weakness, then consult the upstream advisory, issue, and fix to determine the affected behavior and required change. A vulnerability category alone does not establish which checks or configuration changes will prevent exploitation. If the root cause is still unclear, do not assume that a wrapper from [Case 2](#case-2) fixes it.

extra_sources.source_section: Vulnerable Dependency Management Cheat Sheet > Cases > Case 3 > Approach
extra_sources.source_passage:
**Step 3:**

If possible, create a unit test that mimics the vulnerability in order to ensure that the patch is effective and have a way to continuously ensure that the patch is in place during the evolution of the project.

If you have a set of automated unit or integration or functional or security tests that exists for the application then run them to verify that the patch does not impact the stability of the application.

A patch written in-house does not get the benefit of the doubt that an upstream release gets, so hold it to an explicit bar before considering the vulnerability handled:

- The test reproducing the vulnerability fails against the unpatched dependency and passes against the patched one. A test that passes in both cases proves nothing about the patch.
- The tests of the dependency itself still pass, which catches behavior that the patch broke but the application does not exercise directly.
- The alert raised by the detection tool is suppressed per [CVE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_Vulnerabilities_and_Exposures) only once the two points above hold. Suppressing the alert, or changing a version string so that the tool stops matching it, records a fix but does not make one.

Expect the tool to keep flagging the dependency even after a correct patch, because [looking at the version number of a package will not tell you whether the fix is present](https://access.redhat.com/security/updates/backporting). That is a reporting problem to be handled with a scoped suppression, not a reason to change the patch.

question: Django hands you a ready-made `django.contrib.auth` app for login/logout/password stuff, but FastAPI doesn't really have an equivalent. If I use FastAPI's `OAuth2PasswordBearer` helper, does it actually check that the token is legit, the way Django's auth app handles things for me?
answer: No. OAuth2PasswordBearer only checks the authorization scheme and pulls the bearer token out of the Authorization header — it does not validate the token or verify its signature. You still have to write your own authentication dependency that verifies the token and rejects invalid credentials before it returns a user. Django's django.contrib.auth, by contrast, already ships views/forms for login, logout, and password changes out of the box.
source_section: Dependency Injection and Access Control > OAuth2PasswordBearer Does Not Validate Tokens
source_passage: The helper class `OAuth2PasswordBearer` checks the authorization scheme and extracts the bearer token from the `Authorization` header. It does **not validate the token or verify its signature**. An authentication dependency must verify the token and reject invalid credentials before returning a user.

question: If I turn on allow_credentials=True for CORS in my FastAPI app, can I leave allow_origins as a wildcard to save time?

question: I want a Laravel rate limit that's keyed to the logged-in user's ID (falling back to their IP) at 5 requests a minute, instead of just using one of the default throttle numbers. How do I set that up?
answer: Define a custom limiter, typically in RouteServiceProvider, with RateLimiter::for('custom-limit', function ($request) { return Limit::perMinute(5)->by($request->user()?->id ?: $request->ip()); }); then attach it to the route with the throttle middleware, e.g. Route::middleware('throttle:custom-limit')->get('/dashboard', fn () => 'Dashboard').

question: Both Twig (Symfony) and Blade (Laravel) escape template output by default to stop XSS — but each lets you deliberately turn that off for trusted content. What's the 'print this unescaped' syntax in each one?
answer: Twig uses the `raw` filter, for example `{{ product.title|raw }}`. Blade uses unescaped echo tags, for example `{!! trustedHtml !!}`. Use either only for content trusted to contain safe HTML; Blade specifically warns that using its unescaped syntax on untrusted input creates XSS risk.
source_section: Main Sections > Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
source_passage:
Symfony comes by default with twig templates that automatically protect applications from XSS attacks by using **output escaping** to transform variables containing special characters by wrapping the variable with `{{ }}` statement. ```twig

Hello {{name}}

{# if 'name' is '', Twig will output this: '

Hello <script>alert('hello!')</script>

' #} ``` If you are rendering a variable that is trusted and contains HTML contents, you can use *Twig raw filter* to disable output escaping. ```twig

{{ product.title|raw }}

{# if 'product.title' is 'Lorem Ipsum', Twig will output exactly that instead of 'Lorem <strong>Ipsum</strong>' #} ```

extra_sources.source_section: Cross Site Scripting (XSS)
extra_sources.source_passage:
Laravel's [Blade echo statements](https://laravel.com/framework/docs/blade#displaying-data) `{{ }}` HTML-escape ordinary string values using `htmlspecialchars`. This is appropriate for HTML text and quoted ordinary text attributes, but does not validate URL schemes or encode JavaScript or CSS contexts.

Laravel also offers displaying unescaped data using the unescaped syntax `{!! !!}`. This must not be used on any untrusted data, otherwise your application will be subject to an XSS attack.

For instance, if you have something like this in any of your Blade templates, it would result in a vulnerability:

```blade
{!! request()->input('somedata') !!}
```

question: Say my API only authenticates with bearer tokens, no cookies anywhere — do I still need CSRF protection? And does that change if I bolt on a cookie-stored refresh token later?
answer: With pure token authentication and no cookies, you don't need CSRF protection, because the browser has no cookie to automatically attach to a forged cross-site request. But the moment you add a cookie-stored refresh token, that calculus changes: browsers attach cookies automatically, which reintroduces CSRF risk, so that refresh endpoint (and any other cookie-authenticated path) needs real CSRF defenses like validated tokens — treat SameSite as only a defense-in-depth layer, not a substitute.
source_section: Items > CSRF (Cross Site Request Forgery)
source_passage: **Note:** if you use token authentication only, there is no need to protect from CSRF in controllers like this. If cookie-based authentication is used on some paths, then the protections is still required on them.

Protect refresh and other state-changing endpoints with the defenses in the [CSRF Prevention Cheat Sheet](../cheatsheets/Cross-Site_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.md), such as validated CSRF tokens. Treat `SameSite` as defense in depth.

question: When I set up the application cookie for ASP.NET Core Identity, what should I actually configure for HttpOnly/Secure/SameSite, and is there anything HttpOnly won't save me from?
answer: Set Cookie.HttpOnly = true and Cookie.SecurePolicy = CookieSecurePolicy.Always, and choose a Cookie.SameSite value that fits your sign-in flow (test federated sign-in before tightening it). HttpOnly only blocks script access to the cookie itself — it does not stop an injected script from riding along and making authenticated requests using that cookie.

question: What are the actual steps to get CSRF protection working across an ASP.NET Core MVC app, including the AJAX calls?
answer: Register AutoValidateAntiforgeryTokenAttribute globally for unsafe HTTP methods in your MVC app (Razor Pages already have antiforgery protection by default). For any form not covered by that automatic token generation, add @Html.AntiForgeryToken() explicitly. For JavaScript/AJAX requests, send the request token in the configured header or form field, together with the antiforgery cookie.
source_section: Input handling > Cross-site request forgery
source_passage:
- In MVC applications, register `AutoValidateAntiforgeryTokenAttribute` globally for unsafe HTTP methods. Razor Pages provide antiforgery protection by default. These MVC filters are not a substitute for the antiforgery configuration required by other endpoint types.
- Pair token generation with server-side validation. For forms not covered by automatic token generation, use `@Html.AntiForgeryToken()` explicitly. JavaScript requests must send the request token in the configured header or form field, along with the antiforgery cookie.

question: My checkout flow has separate create/pay/confirm endpoints that are each individually authenticated -- what should I do server-side so someone can't just call the confirm endpoint directly and skip paying?
answer: Don't rely on the frontend to enforce call order. Validate workflow state explicitly on the server for every request (model it as a finite state machine), bind tokens or identifiers to specific workflow stages, avoid relying on frontend sequencing logic, and reject any out-of-order transition with a clear error instead of processing it.
source_section: Preventing Out-of-Order API Execution > Prevention Guidance
source_passage:

- Model workflows explicitly using finite states or state machines
- Bind tokens or identifiers to specific workflow stages
- Avoid relying on frontend logic to enforce sequencing
- Reject invalid or out-of-order transitions with clear error responses

question: What controls does the GraphQL cheat sheet list for resource-intensive queries and denial of service?
answer: Add depth limiting and amount limiting on incoming queries, add pagination, set reasonable timeouts at the application and/or infrastructure layer, consider query cost analysis with a maximum allowed cost per query, enforce rate limiting per IP or user, and implement server-side batching and caching (e.g. Facebook's DataLoader).
source_section: Best Practices and Recommendations > DoS Prevention
source_passage:
- Add depth limiting to incoming queries
- Add amount limiting to incoming queries
- Add [pagination](https://graphql.org/learn/pagination/) to limit the amount of data that can be returned in a single response
- Add reasonable timeouts at the application layer, infrastructure layer, or both
- Consider performing query cost analysis and enforcing a maximum allowed cost per query
- Enforce rate limiting on incoming requests per IP or user (or both) to prevent basic DoS attacks
- Implement the [batching and caching technique](https://graphql.org/learn/best-practices/#server-side-batching-caching) on the server-side (Facebook's [DataLoader](https://github.com/facebook/dataloader) can be used for this)

question: If I spin up a grpc-go server without touching any message-size settings, am I already protected from oversized messages, and is that protection enough on its own?
answer: Yes, grpc-go's server-side MaxRecvMsgSize already defaults to 4 MiB with no extra configuration. But that alone isn't enough: a stream can still carry many individually valid messages, so a per-message size limit doesn't bound the total data or processing work for the whole stream.

question: My backend services talk to each other over gRPC internally, and the same system also receives webhooks from an external partner. What do I actually need to lock down on each side of that setup?

For inbound partner webhooks, verify an HMAC-SHA256 signature on every delivery to protect against forged events. These address authentication at the connection and delivery levels, respectively; the exact partner integration may have additional requirements.

source_passage: mTLS provides mutual authentication where both client and server verify each other's certificates, enabling zero-trust communication.

question: In a microservices setup, if the API gateway already checks that a request is authorized before letting it through, do the individual services still need their own authorization checks, the way a REST API checks access at each endpoint?
answer: Yes. Gateway or edge checks only reject unauthorized ingress and complement service-level controls -- they don't establish that a downstream operation is authorized, so each microservice must still enforce its own object, tenant, and business-rule authorization, including on internal calls. This echoes classic REST guidance that access control must be performed at each API endpoint; the difference is that in a monolith that per-endpoint check ran through one shared user authentication/session-management layer, which doesn't hold up once the system is split into multiple composed services.
source_section: Service-level authorization
source_passage: Each service must enforce access to its protected operations, including internal calls. Prefer shared, reviewed policies as the system grows, with service-level enforcement of object, tenant, and business-specific rules. See [Authorization Patterns](Authorization_Patterns_Cheat_Sheet.md#service-level-authorization) for policy placement and [Policy and Data Distribution](Authorization_Policy_And_Data_Distribution_Cheat_Sheet.md) for update and outage handling. Gateway checks complement these controls; they do not establish that a downstream operation is authorized.

extra_sources.source_section: Access Control
extra_sources.source_passage: Non-public REST services must perform access control at each API endpoint. Web services in monolithic applications implement this by means of user authentication, authorization logic and session management. This has several drawbacks for modern architectures which compose multiple microservices following the RESTful style.

question: For service-to-service auth between my microservices, if each service validates incoming tokens by calling the central token service directly on every request, what's the catch?
answer: That's online validation via token introspection, and the catch is it adds network latency and makes every request dependent on the token service's availability. Caching those introspection responses to cut that cost delays how fast you detect revocation, so the cache duration has to stay bounded to the freshness you actually need and must never outlast the token's own expiry.
source_section: Service-to-service authentication > Existing patterns > Token-based
source_passage:
1. Online validation:
    - The microservice queries the token service. For OAuth, [token introspection](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7662.html#section-2.2) reports whether a token is active and can reflect revocation known to the authorization server.
    - Network calls add latency and a dependency on the token service's availability. [Caching introspection responses delays detection of revocation](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7662.html#section-4); bound cache duration to the required freshness and never beyond token expiry.

question: Once a partner's webhook delivery is verified at our edge, it fans out into work across several of our internal microservices -- what should change about how we log that event as it moves from the webhook endpoint into those services?
